title: Rule Extraction Framework
abstract: This document specifies how rules are extracted from śāstric verse into CHOIR: a canonical rule schema with mandatory and derived fields §2 , a Mīmāṃsā-based gate that decides which verses are rules at all §4 , a dual independent extraction protocol with adjudication and a contested outcome §5 , two orthogonal confidence axes set at extraction time §6 , a deliberately conservative unification policy §7 , and acceptance metrics against a gold set §8 . Its governing definition of consistency is that two competent analysts working independently from the same source produce rules that agree on structure, scope, and conclusion — or disagree in a way the framework makes visible and adjudicable §1 . The source document is carried in the repository as Status: Draft for review ; per choir/research/README.md , all 18 research deliverables are drafted, none is accepted, and every document is a hypothesis. This document is drafted but not accepted as specification.

sections.heading: Abstract
sections.html: This document specifies how rules are extracted from śāstric verse into CHOIR: a canonical rule schema with mandatory and derived fields (§2), a Mīmāṃsā-based gate that decides which verses are rules at all (§4), a dual independent extraction protocol with adjudication and a contested outcome (§5), two orthogonal confidence axes set at extraction time (§6), a deliberately conservative unification policy (§7), and acceptance metrics against a gold set (§8). Its governing definition of consistency is that two competent analysts working independently from the same source produce rules that agree on structure, scope, and conclusion — or disagree in a way the framework makes visible and adjudicable (§1). The source document is carried in the repository as Status: Draft for review; per choir/research/README.md, all 18 research deliverables are drafted, none is accepted, and every document is a hypothesis. This document is drafted but not accepted as specification.

sections.heading: Research Question
sections.html:
The source states the brief it answers in §1: "The brief asks how rules can be extracted consistently." It then fixes a testable meaning for consistency rather than leaving it as a claim, in a block quotation:

Two competent analysts, working independently from the same source under this framework, produce rules that agree on structure, scope, and conclusion — or disagree in a way the framework makes visible and adjudicable.

The document is explicit that the second clause carries equal weight: "Some verses are genuinely contested; forcing agreement on them would be a fidelity failure. The framework's job is to make unforced disagreement rare and forced disagreement explicit" (§1). It also states that "Consistency is measured, not asserted — see §8."

A second question runs beneath the first, posed in §3: the brief lists seven required elements (inputs, preconditions, conditions, outputs, exceptions, supporting evidence, cross references), and the framework must map each to schema fields and name its characteristic failure mode.

sections.heading: Finding
sections.html:
The canonical rule schema and what may not be authored

Every extracted rule instantiates a single schema (§2). Fields marked required must be present or the rule is rejected; fields marked derived are computed, never authored. The schema is grouped into Identity, Source, Scope, Quantification, Antecedent, Consequent, Defeat, Evidential role, Relations, Epistemic state, and Process blocks. Required fields include version, the full source block (with edition, attestation graded critical|printed|corpus|quotation|unverified, variant_reading, and character span), the context block, conditions, and a non-empty conclusions list. Conclusions carry a modality drawn from indicates|asserts|obliges|permits|forbids, a polarity, an optional ordinal strength, and an optional named_result (nāmadheya). Exceptions are typed rebutting|undercutting|premise and carry a completeness value of known_complete|likely_incomplete|unknown. Under Epistemic state, the schema annotates ambiguities with the constraint that open items block execution.

The document argues five fields cannot be optional (§2.1):

FieldWhy it cannot be optional
source.editionVerse numbering differs between editions; a locus without an edition is unresolvable (004 §0.3)
context.reference_frame"The 7th house" denotes different things from Lagna vs from Candra; an unstated frame is an unbound variable (005 §6.4)
conditionsA rule with no antecedent is not a rule; it is an assertion
exceptions[].completenessExceptions live in other verses; the compiler usually cannot know it found them all (006 §6.3)
independence_keyWithout it, evidence aggregation double-counts (009 §4)

exceptions[].completeness is singled out: defaulting it to "complete" makes every rule look more decisive than the evidence supports. The honest default is unknown, and moving a rule to known_complete requires positive work — a systematic search of the text for qualifying clauses (§2.1).

Three fields may not be hand-set (§2.2). confidence is derived from structure (001 §3.14); the document's stated reason is that "An extractor who can type a confidence number has an untraceable opinion wearing a number's clothing." id is a content address, and typing it breaks deduplication. strength may record only what the text states (pūrṇa, alpa); an extractor's sense of how important a rule is has no place in the corpus.

The seven required elements and their characteristic failures

§3 maps each of the brief's seven required elements to schema fields and names the failure mode characteristic of it:

RequiredSchemaCharacteristic failure
Inputsvariables, context.reference_frameUnbound variable silently defaulted → over-general rule
PreconditionspreconditionsApplicability confused with condition (§3.1)
ConditionsconditionsImplicit conditionals missed (locative absolute has no particle)
Outputsconclusionsarthavāda extracted as a conclusion; strength invented
ExceptionsexceptionsTyped rebutting when undercutting; completeness assumed
Supporting evidencesource, evidence_class, cross_referencesIndependence not tracked; restatements counted as corroboration
Cross referencescross_referencesUnresolved reference admitted as a warning instead of an error

Precondition versus condition

§3.1 draws the distinction by what failure means, following computational_primitives.md §3.9. A precondition is an applicability gate: failure means the rule is not about this case, no inference is produced, and no evidence is recorded. A condition is a matched requirement: failure means the rule applies but did not fire, which is informative and is recordable as absence-evidence (anupalabdhi) where the context declares completeness. The worked case given is a rule scoped to natal charts evaluated against a horary question — it does not fail to fire, it was never applicable. Conflating the two "pollutes the evidence base with irrelevant negatives and makes explanations misleading" (§3.1).

The extraction gate: not every verse is a rule

§4 applies the Mīmāṃsā classification from vedic_reasoning_methodology.md §4.3 as a three-gate filter, and calls it "the highest-yield filter available":

  • **G1 — Is it injunctive (vidhi / niṣedha)?** Tested by optative/gerundive morphology and conditional structure. A "no" routes the verse to classification and storage as arthavāda, mantra, nāmadheya, or narrative — not a rule.
  • **G2 — Is it self-contained; is anuvṛtti resolved?** A "no" routes to scope resolution or an E-BIND diagnostic.
  • G3 — Are antecedent and consequent both identifiable? A "no" makes it a definition or classification; a "yes" proceeds to EXTRACT.

The document states that G1 removes the most noise: a large fraction of śāstric verse is laudatory, illustrative, or liturgical, and extracting "one with this yoga becomes equal to a king" as a rule with conclusion becomes_equal_to_king "produces a corpus of unfalsifiable superlatives that no downstream machinery can use" (§4). arthavāda is not discarded — it is stored, classified, and available as interpretive context (it often indicates how strongly the tradition weights a combination) and as evidence about authorial intent; it simply does not compile to an executable rule.

The source records a boundary difficulty here: some passages are simultaneously commendatory and injunctive. "Mīmāṃsā has extensive machinery for this and CHOIR does not yet adopt it; such verses are flagged W-ARTHA and routed to review. How much of the classical apparatus is needed is open (004 §8.5)" (§4).

The extraction protocol

§5 states the governing claim that "Consistency is a property of the process, not of the schema. The schema makes consistency expressible; the protocol makes it happen."

Dual independent extraction (§5.1) applies to any rule entering the authoritative corpus: two extractors work independently from the same attested text without seeing each other's output; outputs are compared field by field; agreement advances the rule to reviewed; disagreement goes to adjudication by a third party who records grounds, not merely a choice; and persistent disagreement marks the rule contested, with both readings retained as context-scoped alternatives. The document identifies step 5 as what distinguishes this from ordinary annotation work: "A genuinely contested verse is a fact about the corpus, and recording it as such is more faithful than recording a coin flip." Contested rules can still execute — they produce vikalpa outcomes (conflict_resolution.md §7).

On what counts as an extractor (§5.2): an extractor may be a human scholar, the automated pipeline, or the pipeline plus a reviewer, and provenance records which. Two automated extractions are not independent and do not satisfy §5.1 — they share their failure modes. At least one human extraction is required for accepted status.

Certain conditions route to human review regardless of agreement, because they are the failure modes from sanskrit_analysis_pipeline.md §9 that change what the rule says (§5.3):

TriggerDiagnostic
Ablative/genitive syncretism on a reference-frame termA-SCOPE
Compound classified bahuvrīhi, or type undeterminedA-CMPD
Elision detected but resolved automaticallyA-SCOPE
Possible arthavādaW-ARTHA
Meaning depends on a contested variant readingW-VARIANT
Exception set flagged likely_incompleteW-EXC
Translation-only derivationW-TRANS

Six anti-patterns are explicitly prohibited, "because each is tempting and each corrupts the corpus" (§5.4): harmonising (silently reconciling texts that disagree — destroys the disagreement, which is data); completing (adding conditions "obviously intended" — manufactures rules the text does not state); strengthening (recording a firmer conclusion than the text supports — over-generation, which the document calls "the worst failure", citing 006 §8.2); flattening (dropping context to make a rule more general — produces rules that fire out of scope); merging (combining related verses into one rule — loses independent attestation and separate provenance); and number invention (assigning a numeric strength absent from the text — fabricates precision).

Two orthogonal confidence axes

Two of the three axes from computational_primitives.md §3.14 are set at extraction; the third (inferential) is computed at execution (§6).

Extraction confidence answers did we read it right? (§6.1):

extraction_confidence = min( stage_confidences )        # 006 §10
                      × ambiguity_penalty( open_count )
                      × attestation_factor( grade )
                      × agreement_factor( dual_extraction )

It is "Bounded by the minimum, not the product — a chain is as strong as its weakest link, and stage confidences are not independent."

Interpretive confidence answers does the tradition agree what it means? and is independently sourced (§6.2). Commentarial agreement across ṭīkās, independent attestation in another text via content-address unification, and translation convergence on conditional structure raise it. Recorded commentarial dispute lowers it; a rule known to differ by school lowers it and forces a context split; exception completeness unknown lowers it; and scope inherited rather than stated (prakaraṇa < śruti) lowers it. That last row applies the Mīmāṃsā interpretive priority ordering from vedic_reasoning_methodology.md §5.3 directly as a confidence input: "a condition inherited from context is weaker evidence of meaning than one directly stated. The tradition supplies not just the ordering but the rationale."

§6.3 argues the two axes are orthogonal and must not be collapsed: a verse can be transmitted flawlessly, parsed unambiguously, and still be one whose meaning the commentators have disputed for a thousand years (high extraction, low interpretive); conversely a damaged text whose intent is universally agreed (low extraction, high interpretive). "Collapsing these into one number destroys information a reviewer needs."

Normalisation, deduplication, and the choice of conservatism

Canonicalisation (shloka_compiler.md §8.1) normalises variable naming, condition ordering, equivalent condition forms, and reference-frame expression; two verses that normalise identically produce the same content address and unify. Unification produces one rule with two provenance records — "a genuine independent attestation signal, obtained from the identity scheme rather than a matching heuristic" (§7).

The near-duplicate problem is named as the hard case, with risk running both ways (§7.1):

RelationshipCorrect handling
Exact restatementUnify; two attestations
Restatement with an added conditionSeparate rules; the second is apavāda to the first
Restatement with a different conclusionSeparate rules; a conflict to be adjudicated
Paraphrase, same contentShould unify — but canonicalisation may not reach it
Different rule, similar surfaceMust not unify

The source states the exposure in both directions: "Aggressive normalisation risks merging rows 2, 3 and 5" — the added-condition, different-conclusion, and different-rule rows — while "conservative normalisation misses row 4 and undercounts attestation." The framework chooses conservative: unify only on exact canonical-form identity; surface near-duplicates as candidates for review, never as automatic merges. The stated asymmetry is that "Under-merging leaves duplicate rules, which is visible and fixable. Over-merging silently destroys an exception or a conflict, which is neither." Embedding-based similarity may generate the review candidates (knowledge_graph_spec.md §2.5 permits proposal) but may not perform the merge. The cost of the choice is the one the source names on the conservative side: the paraphrase row is missed and attestation is undercounted.

Measuring consistency

§8 sets the framework's own acceptance criteria, on the stated grounds that "Without these, 'consistent extraction' is a claim rather than a finding."

MetricMethodTarget
Inter-extractor agreementKrippendorff's α per field, over the dual-extraction setReport per field; structural fields should be high
Structural agreementDo both extractions produce the same condition/conclusion shape?The metric that matters most
Scope agreementSame context and reference frame?High required; scope errors are silent
Exception recallAgainst a gold set with known exceptionsLow recall = over-confident rules
Round-trip fidelity006 §8.2 rubricNo-addition criterion is pass/fail
Over-generation rateRules asserting more than the sourceTarget: zero
Gate precisionarthavāda wrongly extracted as rulesMeasured on the gold set

Agreement is to be reported per field, not as a single number: agreement on conclusions with disagreement on context is a very different situation from the reverse, and an aggregate α conceals it. The gold set (100–200 verses, per sanskrit_analysis_pipeline.md §10) must deliberately include arthavāda passages, verses requiring anuvṛtti, verses with exceptions in other chapters, contested verses, and near-duplicate pairs — "A gold set of clean cases measures nothing useful" (§8).

No measurement results are reported. The metrics are specified; the source document records no α figures, no recall figures, and no gate-precision figures, and does not state that the gold set has been built.

Lifecycle

Rules move draft → reviewed → accepted → (contested) → retired, with superseded re-entering at retired and rejected (with recorded reason) as an exit from draft (§9).

StatusMeaningExecutable
draftExtracted, unreviewedNo
reviewedDual extraction complete or adjudicatedSandbox only
acceptedAuthoritativeYes
contestedGenuine interpretive dispute; alternatives retainedYes, via vikalpa
retiredSuperseded or withdrawnNo — but historical derivations remain replayable

Nothing is deleted (knowledge_graph_spec.md I1/I5). "A rule retired because it was mis-extracted keeps its record, because conclusions drawn from it must remain explicable" (§9).

Status of this document

The source is carried as Status: Draft for review. This publication is a drafted research document, not an accepted specification. The programme index (choir/research/README.md) records that all 18 research deliverables are drafted, that none is accepted, and that every document is a hypothesis; MANIFESTO.md states the underlying instruction in narrower terms — "Treat every computational object as a hypothesis rather than an established truth."

sections.heading: Architectural Implications
sections.html:
The schema fixes what a CHOIR rule is at rest, and several of its constraints are binding on components downstream of extraction. Because confidence and id are derived and strength is textual-only (§2.2), no interface may accept an authored value for them; a confidence number that arrives from a human is, in the document's terms, an untraceable opinion. Because independence_key is required, evidence aggregation in the evidence model has the field it needs to avoid double-counting restatements (009 §4).

The precondition/condition split (§3.1) constrains what execution may record. Only condition failure is admissible as absence-evidence (anupalabdhi), and only where the context declares completeness; precondition failure must produce neither inference nor evidence. Explanation output inherits this: conflating them makes explanations misleading.

The gate (§4) constrains the corpus boundary. arthavāda, mantra, nāmadheya, and narrative are stored and classified but do not compile to executable rules. For arthavāda specifically, the source records that it remains available as interpretive context and as evidence about authorial intent, so that material is reachable by the system without entering the executable rule set. The source makes no equivalent claim for mantra, nāmadheya, or narrative.

The contested status is load-bearing for execution, not merely for bookkeeping: contested rules execute and produce vikalpa outcomes (conflict_resolution.md §7), and both readings are retained as context-scoped alternatives (§5.1, §9). Retirement does not delete (knowledge_graph_spec.md I1/I5), because historical derivations must remain replayable — a constraint on storage and on the explainability path.

The conservative unification rule (§7.1) constrains the knowledge graph's identity mechanics: unification is permitted only on exact canonical-form identity, so attestation counts are derived from the content-address scheme rather than from similarity matching. Embedding-based similarity is admitted as a proposer of review candidates and prohibited as a merger.

The requirement that at least one human extraction is present for accepted status (§5.2) constrains any fully automated pipeline: automation can reach reviewed (sandbox-only execution) but cannot on its own produce an authoritative rule under this framework.

sections.heading: Open Questions
sections.html:
The source records six open questions in §10, plus two further unresolved items noted in the body.

  1. Is dual extraction affordable at corpus scale? (§10, item 1) Thousands of verses × two scholars is described as the project's dominant cost. Whether automated extraction plus single review is sufficient for some rule classes — and which classes — is unresolved, and is stated to be the main throughput question.
  2. Who adjudicates, and by what authority? (§10, item 2) §5.1 step 4 presupposes an adjudicator whose grounds are accepted. In a tradition with live disagreement that role is not neutral, and the document says the framework "should probably record the adjudicator's school" — itself a hedged recommendation, not a settled rule.
  3. Exception completeness search. (§10, item 3) Moving from unknown to known_complete requires systematically searching a text for qualifying clauses. Whether this is tractable before the whole text is compiled is called doubtful, suggesting completeness can only be assessed corpus-wide, in a second pass.
  4. Should strength be extractable at all? (§10, item 4) Textual strength terms are ordinal and vary between authorities. Recording them risks false precision downstream; omitting them loses a distinction the text draws. Unresolved.
  5. Cross-text authority. (§10, item 5) When text A states a rule and text B states its exception, whether B's exception applies depends on whether B is authoritative for A — "a question this framework cannot answer" (conflict_resolution.md §5.3).
  6. **Contested rules and vikalpa.** (§10, item 6) Retaining both readings is faithful, but if a substantial fraction of the corpus is contested, execution may produce disjunctions too often to be useful. The rate is unknown until extraction runs at scale.

Two further unresolved items appear in the body:

  • Commendatory-and-injunctive passages (§4). Mīmāṃsā has extensive machinery for verses that are simultaneously arthavāda and vidhi; CHOIR does not yet adopt it. Such verses are flagged W-ARTHA and routed to review, and how much of the classical apparatus is needed is open (004 §8.5).
  • Paraphrase unification (§7.1). Paraphrases with the same content should unify, "but canonicalisation may not reach it" — an acknowledged gap in the conservative policy, with no remedy specified.

No consistency measurements are reported against the §8 metrics; the targets (including the zero over-generation target) are stated as acceptance criteria, not as achieved results.
